key_concept: In an adiabatic process $Q = 0$, so the work done by the gas equals the drop in internal energy: $W = \dfrac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1} = nC_V(T_1 - T_2)$.
steps: Apply the first law with $Q = 0$ for an adiabatic process: $W = -\Delta U = nC_V(T_1 - T_2)$.
For an ideal gas, $C_V = \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1}$. With $\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$, this gives $C_V = \dfrac{R}{2/3} = \dfrac{3R}{2}$.
The temperature drop is $T_1 - T_2 = 60 - 50 = 10\,\text{K}$, and $n = 1$.
So $W = 124.5\,\text{J}$. The work is positive because the gas expands and does work at the cost of its internal energy.
why_not_others: Option (2), 83 J, is $nR\Delta T$: it forgets to divide by $(\gamma - 1)$, which is the isobaric-type expression. Option (4), 166 J, is $2nR\Delta T$, and option (1), 41.5 J, is $\dfrac{1}{2}nR\Delta T$; both use the wrong factor in place of $\dfrac{1}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
common_trap: Writing $W = nR\Delta T$ (giving 83 J) instead of $W = \dfrac{nR\Delta T}{\gamma - 1}$, or multiplying by $(\gamma - 1)$ instead of dividing by it.
time_saving_tip: For a monatomic gas, adiabatic work is simply $\dfrac{3}{2}nR\Delta T$. Here $nR\Delta T = 83$, so $W = 1.5 \times 83 = 124.5\,\text{J}$ directly.
